Copious

/KOH-pee-uhs/ - the stress falls on KOH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Copious means profuse, abundant.

The bride's father shed copious tears before the vows even began — the ushers went through three packets of tissues keeping him presentable.

Worked Example

One hard pruning, and the old apple tree answered with a copious crop: every branch bowed, crates stacked three deep on the porch, and the neighbors learned to cross the street unless they wanted a bag pressed on them.

Copious is the right word because the sentence is about sheer pouring quantity. 'A good crop' states a fact; a copious one arrives in armloads, more than anyone quite knows what to do with. The word's Latin root is copia, 'plenty' — copious things come in plenty, not in portions.

How Copious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

plentiful

plentiful: more than enough, without copious's note of pouring forth

bountiful

bountiful: abundant as if from a giving hand — a word for harvests and gifts

Antonyms

scanty

scanty: too little to meet the need

paltry

paltry: so small it feels like an insult to the need

How Strong Is It? — sufficient → plentiful → copious → overflowing

sufficient vs. copious

sufficient vs. copious: A sufficient supply covers the need exactly and stops there; copious sails past the need without slowing.

plentiful vs. copious

plentiful vs. copious: Plentiful already means more than enough; copious goes a rung further — abundance you measure in armloads and refills.

overflowing vs. copious

overflowing vs. copious: Overflowing outdoes even copious: a copious harvest fills every crate, while an overflowing one spills out of them onto the porch boards.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — copi-

Root — copi-: plenty

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Copi- (plenty, from Latin copia) + -ous (full of) = full of plenty. Roman soldiers drew supplies from the copia, the stockpile of supplies; English kept the plenty and made it an adjective. Copious notes, copious tears, a copious crop — all of them supplies that keep coming.

Use the root in a new word: cornucopia

Use the root in a new word: cornucopia: The harvest-festival poster showed a cornucopia spilling squash, grapes, and wheat across the table.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Copious is the abundance word for quantities that pour forth — notes, tears, rain, harvests. Its unit-mates each stake different ground: replete describes the well-stocked container ('a shelf replete with trophies'), voluminous measures sheer bulk and volume, and prodigious adds a gasp at astonishing size. When the point is simply 'a great deal of it, and more coming,' copious is the word.
